en: Preface to the *Chūgakuki* (Record of Initial Studies) by the Patriarch Hakun.
The *Chūgakuki* was composed by the Patriarch Hakun, Seijaku. Master Seijaku, being a descendant of the former sages, pursued the study of Gautama.
Through words and language, he sought to open the way for the deluded masses and guide those who follow, thereby propagating [the teachings].
This is the essential core of the three vehicles and ten stages, intended to lead beings into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
he was only afraid that people would not become Buddhas, and his heart was thus filled with such earnest concern. Now, for humans to be born in a state of stillness is the nature bestowed by Heaven;

for them to be moved upon being stimulated by external objects is the expression of that nature. Because they are born in stillness, each is endowed with the wondrous subtlety of spiritual intelligence and awareness; because they are moved upon being stimulated, all...
There was the fault of being obstructed and drifting in confusion; the Śākya [Buddha] felt concern for this. He removed their obstructions and brought them back from their wandering.
Whether through exhortation or inducement, whether through intimidation or testimony, he caused them to return to the One Vehicle.

Yet, the sentient beings of the six realms and the heretics of Pāpīyas follow diverse paths; the Buddha supported and protected them with the Right Path through thousands of sutras and ten thousand verses.
Those who shrink from the complexities of practice do so for this very reason. Indeed, "if jade is not carved, it does not become a vessel; if a person does not study, they do not know the Way.

The Patriarch Baoyun expounded and disseminated the teachings to bestow grace upon all beings, enabling them to progress from the first stage (*bhūmi*) to the tenth, until they attain the equal, true, and wondrous enlightenment of a Tathāgata. How could this differ from the Buddha-mind? This is the Baoyun lineage.
The Lord Mingren respectfully presented this for the Imperial Majesty’s perusal;
following its examination, an edict was issued to include it in the Great Canon so that it might be transmitted for all eternity. This, too, is the Tathāgata’s...
He has awakened to the benevolence inherent in all sentient beings. How could I, Mengfu, not feel the utmost joy and offer my highest praise?

I respectfully preface this at the beginning of the scroll. Written by Zhao Mengfu, Imperial Academician of the Jixian Academy and Grand Master of the Central Palace, on the seventh day of the third month in the second year of Huangqing.
The *Chūxué jì* (Records for Beginners).

As for "records" (*jì*), they belong to the category of sūtras and śāstras. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the holy ones and sages of the Three Vehicles either recorded [the teachings] themselves, or...
Regarding past deeds, some accounts describe future retributions; others narrate the origins of transformation in the present age;

and still others extract from the scriptures and laws to directly clarify the Buddha’s intent. These collected texts are titled according to the author’s own intention, such as the Tripitaka of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna compiled by later sages and worthies. However, in the Western Regions, many works are simply called "sūtras."
Treatise: The various titles of the "Records" (Ji) in the Eastern Lands (China) are many, yet their substance is one and the same. What is now called the "Record" (Ji) is precisely this treatise.

Furthermore, "record" (ji) means "to compile" (lu). Because the wholesome dharmas that accord with principle are worthy of being compiled, it records the teachings of the ten stages (bhūmi) of the Three Vehicles to be shown to those at the beginning of their resolve, so that they may practice and study them. Moreover, "record" (ji) also means "response. Those at the beginning of their resolve [desire to]...
The "student" (śaikṣa) asks for instruction on the methods for initiating practice and cultivation; thus, this response is given.

As for the term "treatise" (śāstra), it refers to that which investigates thoroughly through repeated cycles so that the principles and meanings become clear, making it easy for beginners to study and learn. This is what is meant by "the student."
It is emulation. By emulating and practicing without ceasing, one spontaneously attains insight. That which constitutes insight is what is termed "awakening" (bodhi).
Once awakened, one applies oneself to the practice of conduct; when this conduct inevitably reaches its destination, it is called ultimate awakening. Awakening is precisely the Buddha.
However, it must reside in the initial mind; therefore, it is called "beginner's practice" (*shogaku*). This also demonstrates the spirit of not disparaging others.
As the text says: "A single step toward a thousand li is the beginning. This is excellent evidence.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Qingjue of Baoying Monastery in the Western Capital.

This is the title and rank of the author of the record. It consists of three levels of general and specific designations: first, "the Western Capital" is the general designation, while "Baoying Monastery" is the specific;
this is because there were not merely one monastery in the Western Capital. Second, "Baoying Monastery" is the general designation, while "Śramaṇa Shi" is the specific.

This is a specific [designation], for it accommodates the four classes of people. "The three śramaṇas of the Śākya" is a general [term]; "the venerable name of the Patriarch" is a specific one, as there are many sons of the Śākya.
The character *shu* (to record/narrate) applies to both the agent and the object: the Patriarch is the narrator (*neng-shu*), and the recorded text is that which is narrated (*su-shu*).
"Western Capital" is one of the four capitals; it is a place name. Luoyang was [founded by] the Duke of Zhou’s...
Regarding its history: during the Later Han dynasty, the capital was established here. As the Han ruled the world with the virtue of Fire (*huo-de*), the city was renamed Luoyang.
During the Tang dynasty, it retained its former name and was made a subordinate prefecture of Henan. Baoying Temple is situated by Mount Longmen.

The mountain is located to the west of Luoyang. The reason the name of the mountain is not mentioned here but the name of the locality is cited is that "Western Capital" (Xijing) is a designation for a great metropolis;
furthermore, there is also a Longmen Mountain in Yuhang. Baoying Temple is precisely the place where the author of this record received the scriptures.
In the second year of the Xining era, the author paid his respects to Great Master Haihui, went forth from the household life, and received full ordination.
Later, Haihui spoke a verse to encourage him to travel abroad. In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, he hung his staff at Lingyin Temple in ancient Hangzhou.

Monastics and laypeople seeking the Dharma came in great numbers. The abbot, Venerable Lanyan Tong, requested that the Master reside at Baiyun Hermitage behind the temple. On the day of the Master’s birth, white clouds filled the room.
For this reason, he called himself "White Cloud" (Baiyun). The name of this hermitage resonated in silent accord with his mind, and he dwelt therein.
Consequently, the fame of "White Cloud" spread far and wide, becoming increasingly renowned. Furthermore, white is the root of all colors, signifying purity and freedom from blemish.
As for "clouds," they appear through spontaneous application; they come from nowhere, and when their function is exhausted, they depart, leaving no trace.
Wherever it goes, it is able to contain and moisten the rain of the Dharma, benefiting and sustaining all things in inexhaustible layers; thus, it possesses the likeness of clouds.

It extensively expounds the metaphors of the Dharma as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; that the Sage has no name, yet establishes appellations for the sake of beings, so that their resonance is proclaimed throughout the realms of humans and devas, is truly for this reason.
"Śramaṇa" is the general title for those who have left the household life. "Śākyamuni" is the name of his original teacher.

Regarding his lineage: the succession of his dharma heirs has flourished and continued, such that it is fitting to record his full titles. "Upper Purity, Lower Enlightenment" (*Shangqing Xiàjué*) is the honorific name of the author of the *Record*.
His courtesy name was Běnrán; his style was Báiyún; his surname was Kǒng. He was the fifty-second descendant of the Most Sage King Wénxuān (Confucius).
His kinsman Kǒng Xuānyì composed a true eulogy (*zhēnzàn*) which may be consulted for verification. Kǒng Xuán, a jinshi graduate, compiled [this account].
The court officials of the Song dynasty composed several dozen eulogistic essays on various Chan masters, which were published for the world.
The remaining details of their lives are fully contained in their respective biographies. To recount rather than compose is the height of humility.
Annotated by Dao’an, Dharma-heir of Nanshan Great Puning Temple.

The two phrases, "One must study the Buddha-way" and "One must be concerned with birth and death," constitute the general purport of this entire work. The Master of the Record has appeared in the world through the power of his vows. For...
It is for the sake of sentient beings that [the teachings] are composed. The purpose for which the school is established and the doctrine founded lies herein: the Buddha-way (*buddhamārga*).

This is a concise rendering of the correspondence between the Chinese and Sanskrit terms, selected for the sake of explanation. By means of it, one may leave behind poverty and receive wealth and honor; cross over birth and death, and transcend the wheel of suffering.

Although there are differences such as the primary and auxiliary, the provisional and the real, they are all termed the Buddha-way. Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: [...]* *Note: The original text fragment ends with "Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra," indicating the following citation would have continued from that point.*
In the middle [section], the "Chapter on Explaining the Buddha-way" is taught to counteract doubt and attachment. Within the realms of humans and devas, one must not fail to study;

if one does not study, one will remain impoverished, lacking both merit and wisdom, and enter the perilous path of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, the next line says: "One must not fail to be concerned about birth and death.
The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. How could one afford to sit idly by and wait for bitterness?
"Pain. Students of the Way should constantly affix these two characters to the tip of their noses as a method of remedial practice.
The ancients applied their minds with such urgency; how can people today not feel concern?
In vain one wastes this fleeting life; wisdom, instead, turns into folly.
This clarifies the fault of not studying. A person of intelligence is driven by that very intelligence, merely attending to worldly affairs.
Managing worldly affairs and focusing their minds solely on fame and profit, what leisure do they have to seek the Way of the Buddha?
Or perhaps, holding the sacred realm in high esteem while boasting of worldly wisdom and eloquence, they not only waste their time in vain, but instead sink further into the realms of suffering.
One may say they are exceedingly foolish and clumsy.
Do not be surprised that their study of the Way fails to bear fruit;

for while all people of the time throw themselves into the den of heterodoxy, those who inquire and study the Buddha-dharma are by no means few, yet those who achieve success are rare—this is what is meant by "arduous cultivation through suffering."
If one practices without the causes for Nirvana, is this not a case of those who study the Way wasting their efforts? Therefore, I have offered this response:
because they do not attain the correct path, they fail to accomplish the Way.
If you wish not to encounter deception, do not depart from the ten stages of the Three Vehicles.
These ten stages of the Three Vehicles follow a gradual sequence, like a person returning home; if one clearly recognizes the road, one will not be led astray or deceived by others.
Now, the ten stages of the Three Vehicles appear in various sūtras and śāstras, as taught in the *Avataṃsaka*.

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are exclusively the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), as taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. The ten stages as explained in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (or *Tathāgatagotra-nirdeśa-sūtra*) encompass all three vehicles;
therein, those of the three vehicles each have their own ten stages, namely: the ten stages of the Śrāvaka, the ten stages of the Pratyekabuddha, and [the ten stages of the Bodhisattva].
The ten stages of the bodhisattva each have their own names; while the names of these ten bodhisattva stages are the same as those in the *Avataṃsaka*, their meanings differ.
In the present text, the names of the ten stages are adopted from the *Avataṃsaka* while the meaning is modeled after the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Encompassing the various sūtras, it establishes its own system of thought, with the aim of being comprehensive rather than restrictive. Regarding the mention of the "three vehicles," there is also...

There are several types. First, the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the Small Vehicle are called the "Three Vehicles. Second, within the Great Vehicle, the Middle Vehicle, and the Small Vehicle are called the "Three Vehicles";
these refer respectively to Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas. Within this [second classification], there are three meanings.
First, it merges the One Vehicle with the Great Vehicle and unites the two vehicles [Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha] with the Small Vehicle; therefore, [it is said that] only...
Third. Second, within the Mahāyāna itself, there are naturally three vehicles (*triyāna*), as explained in the *Mahāyānāvatāra-śāstra*. Third, within the Hīnayāna as well, there are three vehicles;
as stated in the *Hīnayāna-śāstras*, there are naturally the Dharma of the Śrāvaka, the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddha, and the Dharma of the Buddha.

Question: Since there is already the Dharma of the Buddha, why is it called the "Lesser Vehicle" (*hīnayāna*)? Answer: The "Dharma of the Buddha" mentioned here refers merely to [the practice of] loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The practice of compassionate love differs only from that of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Regarding the three vehicles in the present text, to which category do they correspond?

In the first [classification], they correspond to the second; in the second, they are used in their entirety. Although the third explanation differs according to the capacity of the practitioner, the nature of the teaching, and the metaphors employed, it applies universally across all texts and is not restricted to a single fixed meaning.
Its intent lies in exhorting practitioners to cultivate and realize transcendence from the realm of suffering. However—
This is because one is restricted by the limitations of words and teachings.
If one does not rely upon the True Dharma (saddharma), it is like climbing a tree to catch fish, or like reaching for the moon in a well;
even the Ten Stages and the Three Vehicles constitute this True Dharma. To abandon these and practice otherwise is like seeking fish from a tree branch—it is the way of a monkey.
"Saving the Moon" is a metaphor for those who do not cultivate [the path]. What is the True Dharma? It is as explained in the following text:
The Sudden Teaching of the Wondrous Enlightenment of the Buddha Vehicle; Those on the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi) who are designated as Bodhisattvas; The Pratyekabuddhas of the Five Fruits;
the Arhats of the Four Fruits, Six Supernatural Powers, Three Fruits, Two Fruits, and One Fruit; And those with various outflows (āsrava) who have not yet attained supernatural powers.
Awakening the mind and seeing one's nature through Prajñā—these names and titles refer to the stages of the ten bhūmis within the Three Vehicles.
From the sixth stage, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi, to the ninth stage, the Dharmameghā-bhūmi, constitutes the Bodhisattvayāna.
The fifth fruit preceding these is the Pratyekabuddhayāna. The four fruits of Arhatship...

"Chinese: This refers to the Śrāvaka-yāna. 'Three, two, one, three. Because they have not yet advanced to the stage of a Śrāvaka, yet cannot regress to the rank of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), it is said that while their outflows (āsrava) remain, they have not yet attained supernatural powers (abhijñā). This must refer to the Śrāvaka-yāna at the stages of *darśana-mārga* and *bhāvanā-mārga*.
Regarding the designation 'inner ordinary person' (*adhyātma-pṛthagjana*) for those who awaken the mind and realize the nature through Prajñā: there are two types of Śrāvakas."

Regarding the stages: first, there are two types—ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*). Within the stage of ordinary beings, there are again two: external ordinary beings and internal ordinary beings. External ordinary beings are further divided into three:

first, the five stabilizing concentrations (*pañca-vastu-sthiti-citta*); second, the mindfulness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*); and third, the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*). These three all belong to the stage of external ordinary beings and are also called the stage of provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*).

Those of the human and celestial realms, as well as those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), when first setting their minds upon entering the Path, cultivate these three gates to counteract the afflictions of ordinary beings.

Regarding practice (*śikṣā*): there are four internal ordinary stages, namely *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*. These four are also called the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) and are further termed the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Together with the two external ordinary stages, they are collectively known as the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya-avasthā*). As the text states:
"Those who awaken the mind and see the nature through Prajñā—whether humans, devas, or external ordinary beings—having long since refined themselves within the three dharmas, awaken to Prajñā..."

If the mind perceives the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), exerts itself through diligent application, and proceeds toward the fruit of the noble ones, it enters the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This subsequent stage of the noble ones is also divided into three: first, the path of seeing, which corresponds to the first fruit; second, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It is completed during the second and third [stages], the three paths of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), and finally at the fourth stage, the level of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Question: The text states that those in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are called Bodhisattvas; why then does it here refer only to the sixth through the ninth? Answer:
The ninth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), is what is referred to as the tenth stage in other sūtras. Here, it is simply called the "ten stages."

This is as explained according to other sutras. Question: Should not the Sudden Teaching’s Wondrous Enlightenment Buddha Vehicle be excluded from the enumeration of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Three Vehicles?
Answer: This stage is precisely the fruit that is cultivated; the ten stages of the Three Vehicles are the causes through which one cultivates.
By gradually cultivating the sequence of the ten stages of the Three Vehicles, once the causal practices are perfected, one realizes [the fruit] suddenly.

This is the wondrous awakening; therefore, it is specifically stated here that the Sudden Teaching enters the sudden from the gradual. This is the standard for gradual cultivation leading to sudden enlightenment. Question:

Since it is said that one enters the sudden from the gradual, it would be appropriate to proceed from the small to the great, first explaining the stages of the first fruit and second fruit up to the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
Why, then, has the sequence been inverted in this text? Answer: This follows the order of the Buddha’s [teaching].

The Sūtra proceeds from the fundamental to the derivative, intending to lead students to return to the root and revert to the source; thus it says, "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, one distinguishes and teaches three.
If the fruit of cultivation is not realized, this is entirely due to clinging to emptiness or clinging to existence.
The *Zhengzong lun* (Treatise on Realizing the Source) states: "To realize the Way without realizing the fruit is called the illness of clinging to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

To lecture on the sutras without realizing the fruit is called the illness of clinging to existence (*bhava*). Why is it that throughout the mountain-like heaps of the Tripitaka of the Three Vehicles, not a single practitioner of the Three Vehicles is to be seen?
It is entirely because of the illnesses of clinging to emptiness and clinging to existence. Thus he asks about the Buddha-dharma.

Using the gates of emptiness and existence as means to lead people toward cultivation and practice, those who propagate these teachings may either disparage emptiness while praising existence, or refute existence while praising emptiness;
some claim that emptiness is shallow while existence is deep, while others claim that emptiness is deep while existence is shallow.

Each relies upon their own scriptures and treatises to ripen the capacities and conditions of sentient beings. Apart from these two gates, there is nothing else to rely upon. Now, all of these are regarded as illnesses.
Is it not the case that this does not contradict the sūtras and śāstras? The answer is: what is discussed in the sūtras and śāstras returns to the Middle Way.
To cling to one extreme is the very source of illness; therefore, this is designated as the "illness of clinging to emptiness and clinging to existence."
You must know the source of the Sūtra-piṭaka; I shall now explain it for you. It is not that I, this poor monk, am given to much talk;

beginners must know this in detail, so ask those who practice cultivation. Once you have realized that impermanence is swift, you should immediately and urgently engage in cultivation. However, as yet...

When reading the sutras, one encounters the fundamental principle (the *zong*) as circumstances arise; how can one know for certain that one has not fallen into the dual maladies of nihilism (*uccheda*) and eternalism (*śāśvata*)?
Answer: To understand the source of the Sūtra-piṭaka, I shall now explain it for you. The Master of Records (Jizang) was profoundly compassionate, speaking of his own accord without being asked.
As the ancients said: "Who would say that teaching without being requested is not sincere? Since there was no one who requested it, [he spoke].
"Why need there be so many words? [The Master] replied: "A beginner must know the details. As for the term 'poor monk' (pindao):
when the Buddha-dharma first arrived, all monastics were called 'Daoists' (daoshi). They referred to themselves as 'poor Daoists. Now, we follow this ancient usage."
It is like a bright mirror placed before one, which clearly reflects the right and the wrong of the past and the present;

this analogy makes it easy to see. However, while the mirror in the analogy merely reflects beauty and ugliness, or length and shortness, what is here called "the right and wrong of the past and present" is explained in terms of the Dharma.
Countless Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have appeared, yet this matter has never been altered or changed.
"Countless" refers here to the sands of the Ganges. Reflecting upon the Buddhas of the past, they too should have preached the Three Vehicles;
for the Way of every Buddha is the same—dare anyone alter or change it?
In studying the Way, first seek the causal ground; the fruit-stage is simply the culmination of cultivation.
If the fruit is not fulfilled and merit is not perfected, then even if one is eloquent and swift of tongue, it certainly has nothing to do with the True Dharma.
The first three lines concern the actual efficacy of cultivation; the latter two lines are merely empty formalities. Furthermore, the first two lines concern the cause.
The mind that realizes the ground must correspond with the designations of the fruition stage; the latter three phrases are all expressions of reductio ad absurdum.
Beginners should first seek the causal ground.
The two characters "ground" (*bhūmi*) establish the name through both dharma and metaphor. A ground is capable of generating and supporting; if there were no seeds, nothing would be produced.
Among those who practice, there are none who do not take the arousal of the mind as the cause. By arousing the Mahāyāna mind, one attains the fruit of Mahāyāna;
by arousing the Hīnayāna mind, one attains the fruit of Hīnayāna. It has never happened that one arouses a small mind and yet attains a great [fruit].
Regarding the fruit: therefore, a sutra says, "If the ground is not straight, the fruit will be crooked.

The Master of the Commentary (Jizhu), deeply fearing that the minds of beginners might not be purified through correct means, specifically stated here: "Beginners must first seek the ground. As for the word "study" (xue), it is like adornment.
If a vessel is not adorned, there is nothing by which it may be beautiful to behold; if a person does not study, there is likewise [no beauty].
Because he possessed such sublime virtue: as for those who study, they increase daily; as for those who cultivate the Way, they diminish daily.

By diminishing, one’s achievements in the Way surpass all heights; by increasing, one’s labors in study extend ever further. Thus, his physical form was forever separated from that of common people, and his mind stood in stark opposition to worldly sentiments.
"First, one practices through precept, concentration, and wisdom.
One must know that the first phrase provides a general heading, while the second phrase gives rise to the meaning of the subsequent text.

Since the title speaks of "beginners," and these three dharmas are placed at the head of the treatise, one should know that all three are called "learning" (*śikṣā*). For a person who has first begun their practice, it is essential...

Taking these three dharmas as the causal ground is to establish the threefold right training in contrast to the threefold wrong training of the world’s long-standing heterodoxy, thereby counteracting it.
It also demonstrates the intention of turning away from heterodoxy and returning to the correct path. Precepts serve to prevent wrongdoing and cease evil;

concentration serves to still discursive thoughts and quiet external conditions; wisdom serves to shatter delusions and realize the truth. These three dharma-gates should all be practiced accordingly.
Cultivation and study. This is the gateway to cultivation and study; it follows a specific sequence. Thus, a sutra says:

"By relying on this precept, one attains the various dhyāna-concentrations as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering. Why is this so? The actions initiated by body and speech are governed by the defense of the precepts.
When the three poisons erupt, they necessarily arise from the mind. Now, first one seizes them with the precepts, and subsequently binds them with concentration.
Finally, they are extinguished by wisdom; this sequence is indeed logical. Furthermore, these three dharmas are precisely the meanings elucidated by the Tripiṭaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
For those who study universally, it is the fundamental intention of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to cause people to train in the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
therefore, they employ the three teachings of the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Tripiṭaka to elucidate and demonstrate them. Thus it is said:
The three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) do not consist merely in studying written words and verbal teachings. Therefore, throughout the various teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, it is said:

"the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), the training in higher concentration (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), and the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*"; they do not speak of a "training in higher sūtras" or a "training in higher vinaya.
The title states: "In the beginning of study, first seek the causal ground," which is immediately followed by ethics, concentration, and wisdom.
There is indeed a profound reason for this cultivation. The names and categories are as explained in the following text:
The fragrance of the fivefold precepts perfumes the body; A single word encompasses ten thousand sections. In the Hīnayāna, one practices by means of the Four Noble Truths;
For Pratyekabuddhas, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; Bodhisattvas must practice the Six Pāramitās; And in the Buddha Vehicle, all are arranged throughout the ten directions.
The five parts are precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
These transform the physical body of the five aggregates into the fivefold Dharma-body. One distinguishes between the mundane and the supramundane;

now, as for these five fragrances all being called "precepts," it is because precept is the beginning and arises from precept. Thus, the single character "precept" (śīla) encompasses everything. Therefore—

The subsequent line states: "A single word encompasses all ten thousand sections. Although it is said that this single word universally subsumes all categories, its applications differ according to the capacities of sentient beings;
thus, the following text says: "In the Hīnayāna, they are termed the Four Truths and so forth.
However, these truths, conditions, paths, and powers receive different names depending on the three vehicles and the Buddha. In reality, they all arise from within the precepts.

Dharma’s *tāi-xī* (embryonic breath) meditative concentration: taking one step across a thousand li as the beginning. Upon reaching this, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) is established, forming the foundation for the inner stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

The first phrase correctly clarifies the essence of the concentration; the second phrase clarifies its essential meaning; and the final two phrases describe the attainment of the name upon the completion of the practice.
Furthermore, as for what is called "embryonic breath" (*tai-xi*), it is a name established by means of a metaphor. The metaphor is this:

when sentient beings first enter the womb, they possess but a single breath that sustains the mass of flesh; gradually, this grows until it takes form and emerges from the womb. At that time, one cannot yet distinguish between good and evil.
So too, the practitioner of dhyāna-samādhi holds the mind to a single point—whether it seems to exist or not to exist—and all things, whether good or evil, do not [disturb them].

Contemplate this until the practice is perfected; it does not depart from the very first thought-moment. Therefore, the subsequent text says: "A single step toward the thousand-li journey is the beginning.
Reaching this "Stage of Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and its fulfillment—this stage is originally the first among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of a bodhisattva.

Both the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Ratnakaranda-śrī-vyūha-sūtra* share this name. It is situated within the three levels of the "Sages of the Three Stages": Dwelling, Practice, and Direction (*sthiti-caryā-pratipatti*).

Regarding the subsequent term "inner ordinary beings" (*antarāpṛthagjana*): some refer to the three stages of worthiness (*triyānika-śaikṣa*) as inner ordinary beings and the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) as outer ordinary beings.

Since it has already been stated that the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) is attained [at this point], why is it further called "inner ordinary beings"? Answer: This refers here to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).

This is not the same as the "Garland of the Avataṃsaka. One who is called "Joyful" (Nanda) is at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), who is precisely about to resolve their mind to aspire to and enter the Path; thus, they receive the name "Joyful. As the Sūtra says:
"If there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness, well-cultivated various practices, and even give rise to such a mind, they immediately transcend the ordinary."
Regarding the stage of the "inner ordinary person" (*adhyātma-prthagjana*): among the four stages of the Hīnayāna, the initial stage of skillful means (*upāya*) is divided into two.
First is the outer ordinary person (*bāhya-prthagjana*), consisting of the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*) and so forth. Second is the inner ordinary person.

[In this context,] one who abides in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) has accomplished much joy and much pure faith, yet they have not even yet entered the first fruit (*srota-āpatti-phala*), let alone the initial stage of the Bodhisattva grounds. Thus, the term "inner ordinary person" is used.

Regarding the four stages of application (*prayoga*) and so forth: it is only from these four stages of application that one enters the first fruit, which is called the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This refers precisely to the śramaṇa of the path of seeing mentioned below.
The Four Truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—are the support for True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Prajñā. Sound and form equally contain the *dharmatā*.
As the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* says:
"The śramaṇa who has seen the Path. Previously, the truths, conditions, and deliverances were allocated to the three vehicles; why now do you mention only the Dharma of the Four Truths?
The *Zhengzong lun* (Treatise on Proving the Thesis) states: "The commencement of practice consists of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

One should know that the Four Noble Truths are the point of entry for a beginner practitioner. Subsequently, the twelve links of dependent origination and the myriad practices of the six perfections, though their names differ, do not transcend this Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; True Suchness and Prajñāpāramitā likewise rely upon and are identical with sound and form."
Regarding those who embody the true nature (*dharmatā*): practitioners who deeply contemplate the Four Noble Truths achieve the realization of the marks of the Path (*darśana-mārga*).

As the Sūtra says: "The śramaṇa who has seen the Path. Previously, this was referred to as the "inner ordinary person" (*antara-pudgala*), which belongs to the stage of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*).

Now, this properly constitutes the stage of seeing the Path (*darśana-mārga-bhūmi*). What follows below is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-bhūmi*). Because one has actualized the vision of the Path, it is only then called "true cultivation. That is to say—
This is the meaning of awakening first and then practicing. All the sūtras and śāstras of the Hīnayāna speak in this manner.

Once one knows that from the attainment of the [first] bhūmi onwards, the four fruits of the *śrāvaka* arise gradually; that the *dharmadhātu*, the principle (*li*), and the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the *Avataṃsaka* are of one essence as the three bodies (*trikāya*);
and that the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and Dharma-characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are distinguished and the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) and Buddha-mind (*buddhacitta*) are synthesized.
"Whether sentient or insentient"—the first phrase traces back to the preceding text.
The second phrase refers to the two types of retribution: the primary (the body) and the secondary (the environment), as explained in the subsequent text.

Regarding the statement that the first fruit attains the first dhyāna and the second fruit attains the second dhyāna, and so forth, the current mention of "the four fruits in the first dhyāna" cites the first and the last [to represent the whole].

This also encompasses the intermediate stages. Since there is the term "gradual," entering and realizing the stages step-by-step until reaching the ultimate fruit all proceeds from the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding the principle and phenomena (*li-shi*) of the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm: the four dharma-realms of the *Avataṃsaka* do not transcend the two gates of principle and phenomena.
The three bodies are one essence; nature and appearance are discussed in conjunction; and this applies to both the sentient and the insentient.
All share the same wondrous function; these are all signs of the completion of merit and the realization of the ultimate.
The Daoist’s alternative title is "Vast Emptiness" (Xuwu); the divine immortals call it "Primal Qi" (Yuanyang). In the process of transformation, the tiger and dragon intermingle;
Qian and Kun are the female and male principles of Li and Kan. Hasten to cultivate your nature and nourish your spirit; to advance the fire, you must first refine yourself.

The primordial qi of emptiness and non-being emerges from the same source yet bears different names. The practice of the "tigers and dragons" mating is, for those of the Daoist school, a technique for preserving the physical form and attaining eternal life.
According to tradition, the Celestial Master sought the method for ascending to heaven on a white day at Mount Longhu;
his methods of refining elixirs and medicinal herbs, as well as his incantations for water and fire, originated within the stone caves of that mountain.
Though it is called profound and mysterious, it cannot avoid the cycle of saṃsāra; if one does not advance in cultivation, it will ultimately fall into decay.
Confucius spoke of the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) and the Great Primal (Tàisù); Mencius cultivated the "vast breath" (Hào) as the truth;

Zhuangzi entered the silence of the "limitless" (Cānláo); and Lǎozǐ taught that all things return to their root. There are many such various names and designations, yet in reality, there is neither form nor name.
The *Zhouyi Jiuming jue* states: "Before heaven and earth were divided, it was called the One Qi (One Breath).
Within this, there evolved five phases, namely Taiyi, Taichu, Taishi, Taisu, and Taiji. The present mention of Taiji and Taisu does not follow their sequential order;
rather, these two names are cited for illustrative purposes. Although this is not the word of Confucius himself, it nonetheless follows the tradition of the Master.
Regarding your question on "instruction," Mencius said: "I am skilled at nourishing my *haoran* (vast and unyielding) qi, which fills the space between heaven and earth.
This passage from the *Zhuangzi* refers to the state of profound stillness; it records the family tradition as they expounded this Way. Laozi said:
"The myriad things, in their profusion, each returns to its root. In principle, these are all merely provisional names; fundamentally, they have no form.
Such is the state of affairs.

The Great Way must be divided into the Ten Stages; only by distributing it equally can the Three Vehicles be formed. Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism are divided into three teachings, and their scriptures are as infinite as the mountains and seas.
If one can subsume them all within the Way and its Virtue, then the myriad households and thousand gates will be rendered laborious in vain.

Counting the sands with the fingers of words and numbers, [the Buddha] unifies the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism through the Buddhist teaching of the Three Vehicles and the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). As for the reason for this unification: Confucianism provides the foundation for the precepts (*śīla*), while Daoism assists in *dhyāna* (meditation).
Although their gateways differ, their ultimate aim is one; it is also shown that the ocean encompasses the hundred rivers, gathering them all completely within itself.
This is the meaning [of the verse]. The first two lines present the root in its totality. The next two lines differentiate the total into particulars.
The following two lines sublate the derivative by means of the root. The final two lines gather the derivative back into the root.
Regarding the first fruit of *srotāpanna* and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), by whom were these established? There are two meanings.

The preceding nine positions are established through the karmic practices of sentient beings of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) according to the gradual teaching (*anupūrvika-śāsana*), while Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rely upon them to maintain and sustain them. The tenth position is [established through] the sudden [teaching].
Teaching: The Mahāyāna is established through the vows and practices of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, upon which sentient beings rely for their sustenance.
Question: The subsequent sections largely rely on the system established in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Since the tenet of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the convergence of the three vehicles into one, why is it that here only the three vehicles are mentioned, without reference to the One Vehicle? Answer: The sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna is itself the One Vehicle. [This] converges...

The first three vehicles are subsumed within the single Buddha-vehicle. Thus, a sutra states: "Initially, one guides sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, and subsequently delivers them solely through the Great Vehicle.
Although the present text mentions only the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*) and not the "Single Vehicle" (*ekayāna*), this is for two reasons:
first, to accord with the wording of the sutra; second, because the school’s own system is based upon the three vehicles. Question: Regarding this sudden teaching of the Great...
Regarding the "Vehicle"—that is, the One Vehicle—is it situated outside the ten stages (*bhūmi*), or is it situated within the ten stages? If this were so, what fault would there be?
There are faults in both cases. If one says it is within the ten stages, since it is already stated that the ten stages belong to the three vehicles, [how could the One Vehicle be included therein?]
How can there be a One Vehicle (Ekayāna) in addition to the Three Vehicles?

If it is said to be outside of the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi), since one has already spoken of the Three Vehicles and the Ten Stages, how can it further emerge outside of the Ten Stages? Answer: According to the present text:
That is to say, within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), although it is called the "One Buddha Vehicle" (*ekabuddhayāna*), this refers to the single point to which the three vehicles converge;

it is also the manifestation of the One in contrast to the Three. According to the *Zhengzong lun* (Treatise on the Proof of the School), the Wondrous Enlightenment Great Vehicle (*miao-jue da-sheng*) corresponds to the eleventh stage.
The ten stages of the three vehicles are all collectively subsumed within the Sudden Teaching Great Vehicle; this is the convergence of the gradual teachings.
This is the meaning of returning to the point of rest. The Master of the Record provides two different texts, both of which possess their own logic.

Regarding the first, the fruit of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), this is the first fruit within the Śrāvaka vehicle; it corresponds to the second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*), among the ten stages of a Bodhisattva.
The next two fruits correspond to its third stage, and the third fruit corresponds to its... [fourth stage].
The fourth stage consists of the four fruits; this is its fifth stage. The five fruits of the pratyekabuddhas constitute its sixth stage.
The sixth is the entry into the bodhisattva vehicle, which is its seventh stage. The seventh is its eighth stage.
The eighth is its ninth stage. The ninth is its tenth stage. The tenth is designated by the name *Miaojue* (Wondrous Enlightenment) stage.
If this is so, what is the reason for placing [the stage of] Perfect Enlightenment outside the ten stages of the Bodhisattva?

Why is the first Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) bypassed, with the second stage made the first, continuing until the tenth stage is made the ninth, and then Perfect Enlightenment added to complete the number ten?
Answer: There is a profound intention behind this. The first Stage of Joy is the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), which is the beginning of supramundane realization.

Foundation. Based upon this, the Bodhisattva cultivates the three trainings (*triśikṣā*). Within these three trainings, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is placed first. The second stage, the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*), precisely represents the maintenance of ethical discipline.
Since the causal ground is said to begin with the cultivation of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is taken as the initial stage.
Furthermore, the first stage, the Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), represents generosity (*dāna*); however, generosity is not... [text ends].
That which is esteemed by those who have left the household life is that for one who has left the household life, the practice of the precepts (*śīla*) must come first. A question arises:

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is taught that there are ten stages (*bhūmi*), where the "Stage of Dry Wisdom" is the first, the ninth is the Bodhisattva stage, and the tenth is named the Buddha stage; these are called the "Ten Stages Common to the Three Vehicles.
Why not employ this system instead, rather than establishing names by increasing or decreasing the number of the Bodhisattva stages? Is there such a precedent?

No. In the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*, among the eighteen stages of abiding (*vihāra*), the seventeenth, the stage of realizing the path (*mārga-prativedha-vihāra*), is correlated with the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Within the eighteenth stage, the superior seeking of the Buddha-ground (*buddha-bhūmi*), the purity of the buddha-field is fully perfected;

therein, the second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*), is designated as the first, continuing up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*) as the ninth, and the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samantaprabhā*) as the tenth. This serves as the precedent for this case.

The same applies here. Furthermore, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva encompass the causal stage of Buddhahood; since those of the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, śrāvakas, humans, devas, and so forth are all included therein, they may be cited accordingly.
When the holy masters establish their teachings, they do so based on what they have personally realized; thus, one must not be restricted by the specific source from which a teaching originates.
Advancing toward and practicing for one fruit, one invariably realizes a portion of the *sambhogakāya* (reward body).

Regarding the statement that "one layer of bodily radiance appears and a portion of defilements is removed," as for "fruit" (*phala*) and "direction" (*mukha*): "fruit" is the recompense for the cause of advancing toward it; "direction" is the act of moving toward the fruit. Therefore, they are joined.
First there is the direction toward [the goal] and subsequently the fruit. That it is not so now is because the intention lies in the fruit;

thus, the cultivation and the realization of the fruit do not occur simultaneously. All take suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as the basis for progress and cultivation, as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
One who realizes a portion of the *saṃbhogakāya* is called a "perfectly complete *saṃbhogakāya*" after the ten stages have been fulfilled through this gradual process.

Therefore, in the *Meditation on Amitābha*, when one prostrates to the "Pure Ocean-like Assembly" (*viśuddha-samudra-gaṇa*), the collective name for those whose two adornments (*dvividha-saṃbhāra*) are perfected is "the body with its parts fully complete.
That is to say, from the first through the ninth [stages], they are all called "parts" (*aṅga*); only upon reaching the tenth stage does one attain the title of "complete" (*paripūrṇa*).
Because one directs the mind to prostrate universally, it is called the "Pure Ocean-like Assembly. Regarding the phrase "one layer of bodily light appears," the word "layer" (*chóng*)...
It should be pronounced with the third tone (rising tone), which signifies "not slight.

If it were taken as having the meaning of the first tone (level tone), then "one layer" and "two layers" would express the sense of successive layers—just as when one speaks of one lamp, two lamps, up to hundreds of thousands of lamps, each subsequent one is increasingly bright.
The removal of even a single portion of dust and defilement is precisely the second stage, the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Having reached this stage, one naturally knows for oneself that breaking the precepts is a transgression; therefore, by nature one abstains from killing, stealing, and so forth.
This nature is inherently spontaneous and does not depend on human instruction; thus it is called "free from defilement," meaning one is free from the defilement of violating the precepts.
He then transcends the six heavens of the desire realm. Those who have already attained the minor fruit of the first dhyāna within the six heavens of the desire realm are:
first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; third, the Yāma Heaven; fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven;
fifth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and sixth, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. These six heavens have not yet abandoned desire.
Because of the mind, it is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Now, the Srotāpanna has already entered the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*) and has already severed the mind of desire;
therefore, it is said that he "transcends the small fruit of the First Dhyāna. It is not that the First Dhyāna itself is a small fruit; rather, the small fruit is attained within the First Dhyāna.
The first dhyāna has three heavens: first, the Brahmakāyika; second, the Brahmapurohita; and third, the Mahābrahmā. Regarding what is called the "first dhyāna":
there are four levels of dhyāna, and this is the first, hence it is named the first dhyāna. In the Sanskrit language, *dhyāna* is translated here as *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight).
"Quietude" (*jing*) is concentration (*samādhi*). Concentration is able to give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, a sutra says: "Without recourse to *dhyāna*, there is no wisdom.
For this reason, these three heavens constitute the land for the enjoyment of the physical bodies of those who have attained the first fruit of the path.

Seeking neither worldly fame nor profit, and unstained by the adventitious dust of afflictions, one who throughout the day maintains the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* is established therein as a *srotāpanna*.
Having already entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*), though their outflows (*āsrava*) have not yet been entirely eliminated,
they shall undergo seven more returns among humans and devas before gradually entering *nirvāṇa-with-remainder*.
The first three phrases contrast [this state] with what precedes it to manifest its superiority; the latter three phrases contrast it with what follows to reveal its inferiority.
The middle two phrases formally establish the name of the fruit. Having entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*), one no longer pays heed to such petty names as "fly" or "snail.
That all sentient beings fail to achieve the fruit of sainthood is entirely due to being misled by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*). Now, being unstained and unattached, one naturally...

It turns its back on the dust of the mundane and accords with awakening. In Sanskrit, *srotāpanna*; in this [language], it is called "entering the stream. "Entering" means to go into; "stream" means a category.

Because one has already entered the category of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is so named. Regarding the term "all outflows" (*āsrava*): the word "all" implies more than one, yet in brief there are three, namely:

the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*). As for "outflow," it refers to the active manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*) that cause the mind—
Flowing and dispersing continuously without ceasing, it is called an "outflow" (*āsrava*). Like a leaking vessel or a leaking house, it is deeply loathsome;

its defilement and pollution are extensive, and because of its faults and reproach, the name "outflow" is established. Since these have not yet been completely eliminated, humans and devas cannot escape them.
Regarding the term "seven returns": it means coming seven times among humans and being born seven times in the heavens, like a snake that dies after seven steps.
Because the power of their venom is fixed, the first three fruits are all termed *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder); thus it is said they "gradually enter.

Fearing that small vessels are easily filled, do not boast before others. Vow to seek unexcelled *bodhi*, so as to quickly reach the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and the state of an *anāgāmin*; this is the further shore of birth and death.
The first two lines admonish one against self-exaltation; the latter three lines encourage further cultivation.

At the time of death, auspicious signs appear: extending a single finger directly to point it out to others, and the corpse neither stinks nor decays—this has always been the manifestation of the Dharma as it is.
This is the attainment of the *manomayakāya* (mind-made body); herein, the essence of the Way gradually increases and deepens.

Through diligent cultivation of the auspicious signs that assist the Path, one is not entangled by illness; this is what is meant by "passing away while seated or standing. It is a single pointing that instructs others.

This indicates the attainment of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). For the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), two fingers are extended; for the third fruit (*anāgāmin*), three fingers are extended—one should understand this by analogy.
The corpse does not smell and does not decay, indicating the attainment of the first fruit. Therefore, it is said that from the outset, the manifestation of the Dharma has always been thus.
There are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*): first, the mind-made body of the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi, because its power functions according to one's will;
second, the mind-made body of the realization of the self-nature of dharmas, because it manifests at will in accordance with principle and with mastery.

The third is the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya) that arises simultaneously with the three types [of bodies] and is without volitional effort; it manifests according to circumstances and responds to capacities because the mind is sovereign.

All the aforementioned [bodies] are designated as "mind-made bodies" because, in relation to future Buddhas, they are still within the realm of birth and death, yet in relation to those who precede them, they are not inferior. Thus they are named mind-made bodies.
Now, this meaning corresponds to the first type. "Yili" (迤邐) signifies the sense of gradual progression through successive stages. Regarding the "auxiliary path" (*sādhana*), there are two senses.

Speaking in general terms, with the exception of the three vehicles and the ten stages which constitute the "direct path," everything else is an auxiliary path, such as the six daily practices and so forth.
Second, it refers to the wondrously enlightened Buddha-vehicle of the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*) mentioned later. This is...
Regarding the true path, from the first to the ninth stages, all are auxiliary paths (*pakṣa-dharma*). The former interpretation is superior. Why?

Because the text states that "diligence (*vīrya*) concurrently cultivates the auxiliary paths," which implies that for one who practices diligence, apart from these three vehicles and ten stages, [all other practices are auxiliary].

Furthermore, one cultivates a hundred practices, all of which serve as aids to the Path. This is like the Chan Master Shou, who one day performed one hundred and eight kinds of skillful means, and so forth.
Second is the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner).

*Sakṛdāgāmin* is a Sanskrit term; in this [language], it is translated as "Abiding on the Ground of Thinning" (*tanubhūmi*). It is also called "One Who Returns Once. Regarding the designation "Abiding on the Ground of Thinning":
it refers to the noble ones of this second fruit who have already abandoned the six grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.
Because their afflictions have become gradually thinned, they are said to "abide on the ground of thinning. It is also called "One Who Returns Once," as explained in its original context.

Advancing toward the second fruit and the second stage of application, one realizes the two parts of the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body). As for the appearance of the light from these two bodies, this corresponds to the "Radiant" (*prabhākari*) stage;
the first three lines may be understood by analogy with the preceding section. What is called "Radiant" refers to the second [stage] among the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva.
This is the third stage.
It is solely through self-awakening and self-knowledge that one must never boast to others of being a sage of the fruit-stage.

One who manifests as an ordinary person by means of skillful means and engages in the same activities as commoners does so with the intent to gather in and transform sentient beings; ultimately, [it is not for the sake of personal fame].
To say "I am truly a bodhisattva" and so forth refers to what is called self-awakening and self-knowledge.

Having already given rise to the status of Brahmakāyika and Brahmapurohita deities, one is then born into the second dhyāna of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). At this stage, the various outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) have not been eliminated;
thus, one must still undergo the stages of "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and "once-returning," or be born among the heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In Sanskrit, this is *sakṛdāgāmiphala*; in Chinese, it is translated as "one who returns once more.

The first two phrases demonstrate its superiority in contrast to what precedes it; the next two phrases reveal its inferiority in contrast to what follows. The final four phrases provide the formal explanation of the name itself.
Within the second dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are three heavens: first, the Heaven of Limited Light (*parīttābha*); second, the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*apramāṇābha*).
Third is the Pure Light Heaven (*Śubhakṛtsna*). These three heavens constitute the lands for the enjoyment of the retributive body. They do not distinguish between the noble and the ordinary;
all possess habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Even those sages who have realized the fruits of the path cannot avoid them, though there are differences in their degree of thickness or thinness.
Therefore, the term "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*) is specifically used here to distinguish [this stage]. The word "or" (*vā*) is an indefinite term;
it indicates that one may be reborn among the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or born among humans. To further confirm the aforementioned meaning, there is one more coming and going.
It is essential to settle yourself in tranquility and not allow worldly affairs to entangle you. Through diligent practice, day by day, let the gold be separated from the ore.

Having already perceived that there is neither arising nor ceasing, and further knowing that there is no self and no person, it is precisely now that you should exert yourself in cultivation to repay the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence, so as to be worthy of the offerings of your patrons.
Having already become a field of merit free from marks, Not only do humans offer congratulations, But gods and ghosts alike revere and honor him.
The first four lines establish the resolve; the analogy of gold ore is raised: Buddha-nature is the pure gold, and afflictions are the impurities of the ore.

One must cause them to separate early on; when Buddha-nature is revealed, afflictions are extinguished. The subsequent four lines describe the accomplishment: the realization of non-arising and non-extinction.
It is true and eternal. It clarifies that there is no self or person, but only Buddha-nature. Regarding the four debts of gratitude (*catvāraḥ ṛṇa*), there are two meanings.

The three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*) are explained briefly. The final four lines concern the "digestion" of offerings: once one's path-practice is perfected, one is capable of digesting and receiving the offerings of the human world.

The two characters for "field of merit" (*puṇya-kṣetra*) are a metaphorical expression; it is capable of being a field for humans to plant blessings. As for the term "signless" (*animitta*), it means not creating [the perception of] existence.
To form the perception of cause and effect is precisely to realize the meaning of the emptiness of the three spheres.
As for human celebrations, one may say that when a single person attains the Way, ten thousand voices proclaim their worthiness.
The third is the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
In Sanskrit, *anāgāmin* means "one who does not return," also called "one who does not come," and also called "one who has emerged from the mire of desire."
"Emerging from the mire of desire" refers to the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Because these two natures are profuse and complex, they are no different from a mire;
since this noble one has now permanently departed from them, it is called "emerging. The meaning of "non-returner" (*anāgāmin*) will be explained below.
However, when the *anāgāmin* is discussed generally across the three realms, there are seven types; when distinguished specifically, they form three categories. [The first] is the desire realm...

There is one type in the desire realm, five types in the form realm, and one in the formless realm. Among the four fruits, the person who has attained the third fruit possesses the most extensive mode of activity (*ākāra*), because this marks the culmination of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).

Advancing through the three fruits and three approaches, one realizes the threefold reward-body (sambhogakāya). At the stage where the light of the three bodies appears, it is identical to the "Blazing Wisdom" (arciṣmatī) bhūmi;
the first three lines follow the same pattern as before, corresponding to the rank of the third fruit. This is equivalent to the tenth bhūmi among the bodhisattva stages.
