Having emerged from the twenty-eight heavens—that is, the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)—this is the land for the enjoyment of this retributive body. "Emerging" means to arrive there. For this reason...
It is the summit of the three realms; because there is no neighbor above it, it is called "emergence" (*niṣkrānta*). This does not mean a sudden, transcendent departure.

It is named Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Mahāyāna. This is precisely the stage of the Dharma Master. Regarding the "white ox-drawn carriage on the open ground," Equal Enlightenment has two meanings:
first, it is "equal," as it is equal to Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-bodhi*); second, it is "grade," as it is compared to...

In comparison to *miao-jue* (wondrous enlightenment), it is still one grade lower; therefore, it is said to be "approximately equal" (*yue deng*). Although *miao-jue* is also called *Tathāgata*, because it is attained through cultivation despite being equal [to Buddhahood], it is also called a *bodhisattva*.
Here, we shall follow the latter meaning. Within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, this name corresponds to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), or it may be combined with *deng-jue* (equal enlightenment).
Regarding this stage, we shall now explain according to this [latter] perspective. Since the subsequent position is designated as "wondrous," [the former is so named].

Because one awakens to the Buddha-vehicle, this stage is metaphorically designated as the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This refers to the true station of the Dharma Master, a term used to distinguish it from the preceding text.
The previous passage stated, "In principle, one should preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings," which was spoken in terms of superior progress.

The description of "a carriage on an open ground drawn by a white ox" is likewise a term used to distinguish it from the preceding text; the previous stage described it as "the carriage of a great bull."
That which was promised among the three carts at the gate was merely a name without reality;
the "ox-cart on the open ground" now spoken of, which is bestowed at the crossroads, is alone the true fruit. This differs from the previous ox-carts in both color and substance.
The twenty-eighth patriarch of the Western Heaven; the lineage of the Buddha transmitted like this lamp of Dharma.
Each one is titled a Bodhisattva, with spiritual powers equal to those of a Buddha. Truly the heart-seal of Śākyamuni, the fruit-stage clearly manifest and verified.
At the time of his passing, he ascended into the void and displayed eighteen miraculous transformations, self-immolating through the fire of samādhi.
The first five lines of the verse, "Like śarīra falling as rain from the sky," verify the Dharma by means of the person; the latter five lines verify the person by means of the fruit.

As for the phrase "twenty-eight generations," this refers to the period from when the Buddha entrusted [the teaching] to Kāśyapa until the present day, transmitted mind-to-mind without interruption through successive generations. Thus...
Upon reaching Bodhidharma, [the Dharma] was transmitted from the West to the East in this land. It is like one lamp transmitting its light to hundreds of thousands of lamps;
as the lamps pass one after another without ceasing, it is said that "the Buddha-seed is like this transmission of lamps.
To speak of the "Buddha-seed" refers to the succession and flourishing of the Buddha-seed. The Mind-Seal is precisely the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*.
These are alternative names. Mind transmits to mind like a seal impressing an object; hence it is called the "Mind-Seal" (*cittamudrā*).

Among the five subsequent phrases, the first provides a general heading, while the latter four serve as verification. Were it not for the direct transmission of Śākyamuni’s Mind-Seal, how could such a thing be possible?
Kāśyapa compiled the Sūtra-piṭaka, encompassing both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. First one must understand the half-stage of the Pratyekabuddha, then speak of the full mind of the Ten Bhūmis.
Only the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue) shares the same lineage; regarding the fruit-stage, observe its relative heights and depths.

When the sages speak and ordinary people listen, there should be no doubt. To cry out and awaken from intoxication is true cultivation; for the ordinary to speak and the ordinary to listen is error and distortion.

The first two lines of the verse generally indicate that sentient beings are made to fall into a state of drowsiness; the next four lines provide a specific explanation; and the final four lines distinguish this from other states. This refers to when the Tathāgata was still in the world.

Those whose faculties are matured are easily disciplined. Once they receive the words of the Honored One, there is nothing that does not resonate perfectly with them. After the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, these teachings will no longer be heard in the final age;
therefore, it is necessary to compile the collections of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Piṭakas to respond to the capacities of those in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Thus, it is stated in the Vinaya: "Among the six past Buddhas, four Buddhas compiled the sūtras and teachings, so that the Buddha-dharma remained long in the world."
Because the two Buddhas did not convene a council for the scriptures, the Buddha-dharma quickly perished. Thus we know that the Dharma taught by the Buddha must be compiled through a council.
Only the correct cultivation of the *Daśabhūmika* [is sufficient]; as for the rest, how could they even be counted on one's fingers? It takes long refinement to achieve success in the Three Vehicles.
In times of contention, people's natures are impetuous; they love what is easy to learn and easy to master. This is just like eating a painted cake—it does not satisfy one’s hunger. Alas!
When the ancient Way has fallen into ruin, it cannot help but arrange the first four lines of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) to manifest the essentials of this school.
The next two lines serve as a metaphor to clarify the error of vain expectations. Hereafter...
The two lines indicate the intent of this composition.
Regarding the tenth stage, the Stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue-di*):

this stage constitutes the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*) of the Mahāyāna. All that preceded it belonged to the Three Vehicles, which were all gradual; it is now termed the "Sudden Teaching" for this reason.
This refers to the stage of the "Primordial Non-existence of Sublime Learning" (*mūla-abhāva-suśikṣā-bhūmi*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).

Out of the Buddha’s compassionate intent, he accommodates those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), allowing them to dwell together in the ten stages so as to encourage practitioners of the three vehicles to study the Buddha-way.

Regarding the distinctions between those of the three vehicles and the Buddha, I have carefully consulted the *Tripiṭaka* and the ritual formats for practice; specifically, concerning the casting of statues and the painting of images, [the distinctions regarding] the four fruits (*catur-phala*)...
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas of the five fruits are all practitioners of the Two Vehicles and minor sages;
their sculpted and painted images follow the appearance of ordinary monks to represent those of the Hīnayāna.

As for the Bodhisattvas, the great sages, they wear necklaces, bracelets, and armlets, and crown their heads with flower garlands to represent the great sages who have received their office as Dharma masters. Now, this wondrous...
One who awakens to the Single Buddha Vehicle has hair coiled like a spiral atop the head, a halo of blazing light upon the neck and back, and the *svastika* mark on the chest;
the body is golden in color, signifying the perfection of meritorious practice. For this reason, the name "Sudden Teaching" (*dun jiao*) is specifically established.

As for "Sublime Awakening" (*miaojue*): since meritorious practice is already complete, one attains a brilliant and great enlightenment, transcending both the subject that perceives and the object perceived; hence it is called Sublime Awakening.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, one severs the obstacles of the Buddha-stage and immediately enters wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Therefore, wondrous enlightenment is called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*). The Unsurpassed One is so called because there is nothing further to be severed."
Reaching this is the ten-part *saṃbhogakāya*; it is called "transcending the three realms.
The first phrase refers to the perfect *saṃbhogakāya*, while the second phrase refers to the twenty-eight heavens, which cannot contain it.
Initially, one is enticed by the three vehicles; ultimately, one is delivered by the Buddha-vehicle. This alone is called the Sudden Teaching;

everything below it is entirely gradual cultivation. [The stages are: Joyful, Freedom from Defilement, Radiance, Blazing Wisdom, Difficult to Conquer, Manifesting, Far-Reaching, Immovable, Excellent Wisdom, and Dharma Cloud.
Once the Sublime Enlightenment is finalized, the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten dedications are complete.

The ten stages and the eleventh stage of perfected function constitute the distinction between the sudden and gradual schools. The Buddha’s teaching of the Great Canon of Sutras does not transcend these two terms, "gradual" and "sudden.

Within them, there are differences based on the capacity of the practitioner, the nature of the Dharma, and various metaphors, such as the son who abandons his father and flees, or the man who looks into a mirror and mistakes it for his own head.
This explains the gradual and sudden [teachings] by way of the capacities of sentient beings (*yogya*): the gradual approach establishes five periods, while the sudden approach has no two truths.
It explains the gradual and sudden by way of the Dharma: ascending a nine-story terrace versus cutting a single strand of silk. It explains the gradual and sudden by way of analogy.
Although capacity and teaching require one another, and analogies are used to manifest the Dharma, in reality, they are but a single path. Since their fundamental approaches differ, therefore...
Now, this is divided as follows. The first two lines cite a sūtra to establish the proof. The next two lines have already been explained above.
The following four lines list the names of the stages in full. The final two lines set forth the intent of this teaching. Question:

Why are the stages listed collectively even though the initial "Stage of Joy" (Pramuditā-bhūmi) is not explicitly used in the current text? Answer: It is not that it is not used; rather, the Stage of Joy is taken as the point of entry.

The skillful means of the Path pertain to the stage of the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*); as they have not yet joined the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*), they are not counted [among the stages].

If there were no such skillful means, how could one enter the True Vehicle? Therefore, they are listed again. The final two phrases separately set forth the intent of the sudden teaching of the Buddha-vehicle;

thus, the three levels of worthiness (*trayaḥ śaikṣāḥ*) and the ten stages of sainthood (*daśa āryabhūmayaḥ*) are cited as they converge into the Mahāyāna of the *Avataṃsaka*. The *Tathāgataguhya-sūtra* says: "All that..."

The teachings of the śrāvakas, the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas, the teachings of the bodhisattvas, and the teachings of the Buddhas—all such dharmas as these flow entirely into the great ocean of the treasury of Vairocana’s wisdom. This is a sublime testimony.

Prajñā is Mañjuśrī’s perfection of wisdom; Nirvāṇa is Samantabhadra’s fulfillment of conduct. These represent the succession of Śākyamuni’s seed-wisdom, culminating here in Maitreya’s descent to birth.
Mañjuśrī’s wisdom and Samantabhadra’s conduct each symbolize their respective dharmas; Śākyamuni, however, fully possesses both, having entered the Great [Vehicle].
In tranquil concentration, Maitreya shall descend at once.
The model for the youth Sudhana: To universally visit fifty spiritual friends; Now returning to the Abhirati pavilion, the body of Vairocana is present here.
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this is Sudhana; what concern is it of mine? If one possesses a heart of reverence and admiration, one should likewise train in this way:
resting the body within the treasury of the lotus-ocean, enjoying eternal life in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, seated upon the throne of the Great Jewel Flower King.
The Sovereign Lion roars his lion’s roar; the Buddha is the Great Single Cause and Condition.
Today, having awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, he has entered Nirvana without remainder. He has subdued the hosts of Māras and externalists;

the three bodies and four wisdoms are fully realized, and the eight liberations and six supernormal powers have long been perfected. This is unconditioned, signless liberation; in the ocean of enlightenment, there is neither coming nor going.
The Dharma-body and the Dharma-realm are level and equal; the mind encompasses every atom and every land.
It manifests the six paths, the four births, the six directions, and the inner and outer of heaven and earth. Heaven and earth are the sons and grandsons of the Buddha.
The first two lines describe the land upon which he relies; the next two lines describe the responsive body; the following two lines conclude the work of transformation. Next...

The first two lines describe the perfection of the power of the Way (*mārga-bala*); the next six lines describe the fulfillment of the marks and characteristics of virtue; and the final three lines describe the completion of functional efficacy.

These constitute the marks, characteristics, and activities possessed by the Buddhas in their respective aspects: the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

Regarding the three bodies—Dharma, Reward, and Transformation—they are as explained previously in the context of the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). As for the "four wisdoms," they are formed through the transformation of consciousness (*vijñānapariṇāma*).
These are the Wisdom of Equality, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
The "Eight Liberations and Six Supernatural Powers" are two phrases from a sutra of the Avataṃsaka; the text states: "Attaining the six supernatural powers and obtaining the eight liberations."
These are called the eight fruits of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Because he has been a Buddha from the very beginning, it is said that he "attained enlightenment long ago.

Because the essence of the [sentient] being and the Buddha are identical, it is said that he "manifests through transformation. The six paths (or, as some say, five paths) and the four modes of birth—namely, egg, womb, moisture, and transformation—are all within these three realms, which are now entirely my own. The sentient beings therein are all my children; thus one knows that heaven and earth are...
They are the sons of the Buddha.

To provide scriptural proof, I shall briefly cite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: "At that time, the Brahma kings, together with the various Śakras, the World-Protecting Four Great Kings, and Maheśvara, the Lord of Heaven, along with their retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads,"
With palms joined and heads bowed, they pay homage to me and entreat me to turn the wheel of the True Dharma.

If one merely praises the Mahāyāna of the Buddha while sentient beings are submerged in suffering and cannot believe in this True Dharma—because they destroy the Dharma and refuse to have faith—all of these are passages from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The tenth line says: "Sentient beings are submerged in suffering. There is a version of the text that reads: "Sentient beings are sunk in suffering."
"There is no one who suffers" is a scribal error.
To provide further proof, I shall again cite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Now this triple world is mine; All within it are my children, Whether possessing form or name.
They cannot be compared to the Buddha, Yet in the triple world, he alone is called the Most Honored One."
The first three lines of the "Holy Father of Sages and Mundane Beings" quote scriptural evidence; the final four lines adapt to the capacities of beings.

Having been taught for the sake of the Three Vehicles and the Ten Stages, this constitutes the orthodox transmission of the Buddha-Dharma. May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm universally aspire [to realize it].
"Entering together into the ocean of sarvajñā (all-knowledge)—
this is the exhortation for the circulation [of the teaching]. When the holy masters of the True Dharma establish their teachings, they value their circulation above all else,
so that it may universally benefit future generations and bring remote benefit to all classes of beings."
